intro: Every sacred text lives through its readers. The Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutras are short, dense and old, and for more than a thousand years Hindu teachers have written commentaries to explain them. The great commentators Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva read the same words and founded three schools that are still alive today.

In modern times new readers came: reformers in Bengal, freedom fighters in prison, a monk on a Chicago stage, poets in New England, and a great critic of caste. Each read the texts for a new situation. Some found nonviolence, some a call to act, some a case against injustice, and some a vast philosophy.

In this unit you will learn how commentary works as a genre, compare classical and modern readings of the same verses, and practice explaining each reading in terms its holders would recognize. You will not be asked to choose the correct reading, but you will be asked to argue carefully and attribute every belief.
bigQuestion: Why do careful readers of the same sacred texts reach different conclusions, and how can a student describe those readings fairly?

timeline.t: Brahma Sutras, credited to Badarayana, take shape (scholarly estimates vary widely)
Shankara teaches Advaita, non-dualism (c. 8th c.; some lineages give earlier dates)
Charles Wilkins publishes the first English Gita
Ram Mohan Roy helps found the Brahmo Samaj; sati is banned in Bengal in 1829
Vivekananda speaks at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago
Gandhi writes weekly letters on the Gita from Yerwada Jail
Ambedkar and many followers become Buddhists in Nagpur

words.d: a formal commentary on a root text
the triple foundation: Upanishads, Gita, Brahma Sutras
ignorance, in Advaita the cause of seeming separateness
Vivekananda's teaching of service to people as service to God
Gandhi's nonviolent resistance, holding to truth
Aurobindo's joining of knowledge, action and devotion
the study of how people interpret texts

choices: Explains a root text and argues for a reading
test.why: A bhashya is a formal commentary.

test.q: Which text is credited to Badarayana?
test.why: Tradition names Badarayana as author of the Brahma Sutras.

test.q: Which image does Shankara use for ignorance?
choices: A rope mistaken for a snake
test.why: The rope and snake picture Advaita's view of ignorance.

test.q: Which school pictures the world and souls as God's body?
Which school teaches five eternal differences?
What reading of the Chandogya phrase is found in Madhva's tradition?
test.why: Atat tvam asi, found through sandhi.

test.q: What do Sri Vaishnavas call Gita 18.66?
test.why: They read it as the final verse on surrender.

test.q: What did Ram Mohan Roy campaign against?
test.why: Roy campaigned against sati, banned in Bengal in 1829.

test.q: What did Vivekananda teach as practical Vedanta?
test.why: He drew service from the divine in all.

test.q: Which reader stressed energetic action, not renunciation, as the Gita's core?
test.why: Tilak's Gita Rahasya stressed karma yoga.

test.q: How did Gandhi reconcile the war poem with nonviolence?
choices: He said the war never mattered
He read the battle as an allegory of inner struggle

test.q: Which American writer echoed Gita 2.19 in a poem?

test.why: Gandhi read "Civil Disobedience" in South Africa.

test.q: Which reader argued caste rested on scriptural authority that must be rejected?

choices: The study of how people interpret texts

write.prompt: Choose one passage (tat tvam asi, Chandogya 6.8.7; or Gita 18.66 or 2.47) and explain how three readers, at least one classical and one modern, have read it. Cite the passage and translation, give each reader's reasoning in terms they would accept, and argue why their readings differ.
tips: Quote or paraphrase the passage and name the translation.
State each reading as its holder would, then your analysis.
Explain differences by setting, method and school, not by who is right.
Use terms such as bhashya, Advaita, prapatti and hermeneutics.
